options.metric: Annual number of pedestrians injured in Brooklyn crashes
options.denominator: None; absolute sum of recorded pedestrian injuries
options.reason: Annual injury counts are a clear measure of the reported pedestrian injury burden in Brooklyn.
options.answer: Brooklyn reported 3,641 pedestrian injuries in 2013 and 2,835 in 2025 (22% fewer), but injuries have risen 49% since 2021, so these counts alone do not establish safer conditions.
options.interpretation: This answers whether the annual number of reported pedestrian injuries changed: the count fell from 3,641 in 2013 to 1,905 in 2021, then rose each year to 2,835 in 2025. Absolute injury burden is a defensible way to assess how many pedestrians were hurt, but it is not injury risk per pedestrian or trip because exposure is unavailable. It leaves fatalities and individual risk unanswered. The analysis uses Brooklyn crashes in full years 2013–2025; it excludes 659,713 records with NULL borough among 2,132,218 NYC crashes in those years (30.94%; pedestrian injury and death fields themselves have no NULLs) and excludes 9,700 Brooklyn records from partial 2026 through June 11 (2.006% of Brooklyn records from 2013 through June 11, 2026).

options.metric: Annual number of pedestrians killed in Brooklyn crashes
options.denominator: None; absolute sum of recorded pedestrian deaths
options.reason: Separating fatalities highlights the most severe pedestrian outcome, which can move differently from nonfatal injuries.
options.answer: Reported Brooklyn pedestrian deaths rose from 30 in 2013 to 39 in 2025 (30%); the yearly fatality counts do not show improvement across those endpoints.
options.interpretation: This framing answers whether reported pedestrian deaths changed, showing 30 deaths in 2013 and 39 in 2025, with substantial year-to-year variation. A fatality count is a defensible severity-focused safety outcome, although small annual totals can fluctuate. It leaves nonfatal injuries and risk per pedestrian or trip unanswered because exposure is unavailable. The analysis uses Brooklyn crashes in full years 2013–2025; it excludes 659,713 records with NULL borough among 2,132,218 NYC crashes in those years (30.94%; pedestrian injury and death fields themselves have no NULLs) and excludes 9,700 Brooklyn records from partial 2026 through June 11 (2.006% of Brooklyn records from 2013 through June 11, 2026).

options.metric: Share of Brooklyn crashes with at least one pedestrian injured or killed
options.denominator: All reported Brooklyn crashes in each year
options.reason: Using all Brooklyn crashes as the denominator shows whether pedestrian-harm crashes make up a changing portion of the reported crash total.
options.answer: Crashes with pedestrian injury or death grew from 7.44% of Brooklyn crashes in 2013 to 11.38% in 2025, a 3.94-percentage-point increase, indicating a larger share of crashes involved pedestrian harm.
options.interpretation: This answers whether pedestrian injury or death became more common as a share of Brooklyn crash records: that share rose from 7.44% in 2013 to 11.38% in 2025. The crash-level denominator makes this a defensible measure of pedestrian-harm composition even as the annual number of all Brooklyn crashes changes. It does not measure risk per pedestrian or trip, and it does not show the number or severity of people harmed. The analysis uses Brooklyn crashes in full years 2013–2025; it excludes 659,713 records with NULL borough among 2,132,218 NYC crashes in those years (30.94%; pedestrian injury and death fields themselves have no NULLs) and excludes 9,700 Brooklyn records from partial 2026 through June 11 (2.006% of Brooklyn records from 2013 through June 11, 2026).
